newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Dole take credit for less TV violence.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Dole take credit for less TV violence.

text.p: An independent study announced on Tuesday that violence on American television is on the decline, prompting an election-year squabble between President Clinton and Republican challenger Bob Dole over who deserves the most credit.

The UCLA Centre for Communication Policy found that the number of series on the four major broadcast television networks that had raised frequent concerns about violence dropped in the 1995-96 season from 1994-95. Surveyed were networks ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox.
In addition, violence on made-for-TV movies, theatrical films shown on television and children's series was reported on the decline.
The study's director, Jeffrey Cole, said a third annual report on the 1996-97 television season should determine whether the trend is for real or "just an aberration."
"It is our clear sense that the broadcast networks are committed to this course of action and we hope to see what we think will be continued improvement over subsequent seasons," said Cole.
He was was hastily summoned to Clinton's debate preparation headquarters in Aluquerque from Los Angeles to participate in an event with Clinton to crow about the report.

Eager to take credit, Clinton said he has been working to reduce violence on TV since his first year in office when he pressed broadcast television leaders for a decision to include parental advisories on violent programming.

He said he also pushed Congress to include in its telecommunications legislation this year a provision that the so-called "V-chip" be installed in new televisions to allow parents to screen out programmes featuring sex and violence. He was also instrumental in the networks' decision to begin showing three hours a week of children's educational programming.
"Step by step, working together, our administration, particularly the vice president (Al Gore) and I, have worked to make television better for our families," Clinton said.
Dole, who made two speeches critical of Hollywood's use of sex and violence, grabbed for some of the credit too.

"Bob Dole is proud to have been one of the first to speak out on this issue," said Christina Martin, a Dole campaign spokeswoman in Washington. "By standing up to the Hollywood elite, Bob Dole showed how a leader can use the bully pulpit to change our children's world for the better."

She said that Clinton, on the other hand, "has yet to take on his big donors in Hollywood," referring to entertainment industry leaders who have contributed heavily to his re-election campaign. She pointed out that Clinton's contributions, the V-chip and the children's educational programming, have yet to be instituted.

"If Bill Clinton is serious about getting sex and violence off the TV and out of our children's theatres, he should turn down the Hollywood money and turn up the volume on the call for family-friendly viewing," she said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Dole deserves some credit for speaking out against movie and television violence. But Clinton seemed to be taking a poke at Dole when he said: "It accomplishes nothing to simply rail against violence. That's like yelling at the TV or the movie screen, alone in a room."

Cole, the study's author, seemed to be coming down on Clinton's side. "We acknowledge the leadership your administration has taken on this issue, more than any other presidential administration before," he told the president.
